name: Endocrine Emergencies
sub: DKA, HHS, adrenal crisis, thyroid storm, myxoedema, hypoglycaemia

cards.q: What are the diagnostic criteria for DKA?
cards.a: All three: glucose ≥200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or known diabetes; ketosis with β-hydroxybutyrate ≥3.0 mmol/L (or urine ketones ≥2+); acidosis with venous pH <7.3 and/or bicarbonate <18 mmol/L.

cards.q: Outline initial DKA fluid and insulin therapy.
cards.a: Isotonic saline or balanced crystalloid 500–1000 mL/h for the first 2–4 hours (smaller boluses, e.g. 250 mL, in older adults or heart/kidney failure), then guided by volume status and sodium. Severe DKA: fixed-rate IV insulin 0.1 units/kg/h once K⁺ is at least 3.5 mmol/L; mild or uncomplicated moderate DKA may use SC rapid-acting insulin every 1–2 h in a monitored non-ICU setting. Add 5–10% dextrose when glucose falls below 250 mg/dL (14 mmol/L) and continue insulin until ketosis resolves.

cards.q: What potassium thresholds apply in DKA?
cards.a: K⁺ <3.5 mmol/L: replace (about 10 mmol/h) and delay insulin until K⁺ >3.5. K⁺ ≥3.5: start replacing once it falls below 5.0 mmol/L, aiming for 4–5 mmol/L. Check at baseline, 2 hours after starting insulin, then 4-hourly. Routine bicarbonate and phosphate are not recommended (bicarbonate only if pH <7.0; phosphate if <1.0 mmol/L with weakness or cardiac/respiratory impairment).

cards.q: When is DKA considered resolved?
cards.a: The 2024 consensus prefers β-hydroxybutyrate: resolution when BHB is below 0.6 mmol/L with venous pH ≥7.3 or bicarbonate ≥18 mmol/L (reviewer: confirm against Table 1 of the report); anion-gap normalisation is only a surrogate when BHB is unavailable. Start SC basal insulin 1–2 hours before stopping the infusion.

cards.q: What are the diagnostic criteria for HHS and how is it treated?
cards.a: All four: glucose ≥600 mg/dL (33 mmol/L); effective osmolality >300 mOsm/kg (or total >320); no significant ketonaemia (BHB <3.0 mmol/L or urine ketones ≤2+); no significant acidosis (pH ≥7.3 and bicarbonate ≥15). Altered mental status is no longer required. Fluids first, then fixed-rate insulin 0.05 units/kg/h; limit glucose fall to 90–120 mg/dL/h and sodium fall to 10 mmol/L in 24 h. Mixed DKA/HHS is treated as DKA (0.1 units/kg/h).

cards.q: What are the complications of DKA treatment?
cards.a: Hypokalaemia, hypoglycaemia, cerebral oedema (especially children), hypophosphataemia, and hyperchloraemic acidosis from large saline volumes.

cards.q: How is adrenal crisis managed?
cards.a: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus then 200 mg/24 h by infusion (or 50 mg every 6 h), isotonic saline 1 L in the first hour, glucose if hypoglycaemic, and identify the precipitant. Do not delay for tests.

cards.q: What are the clinical and laboratory clues to adrenal insufficiency?
cards.a: Unexplained hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, abdominal pain; random cortisol <3 µg/dL (83 nmol/L) is strongly suggestive.

cards.q: List the Burch–Wartofsky features of thyroid storm.
cards.a: Fever, tachycardia (often >140), AF, heart failure, agitation, delirium, diarrhoea, jaundice; scoring ≥45 suggests storm.

cards.q: How is thyroid storm treated?
cards.a: Beta-blocker (propranolol or esmolol), thionamide (propylthiouracil or methimazole), iodine given 1 hour after thionamide, hydrocortisone, cooling, and treat the precipitant.

cards.q: How do you treat myxoedema coma?
cards.a: IV levothyroxine 200–400 mcg load (liothyronine optional), hydrocortisone 100 mg 8-hourly until adrenal insufficiency is excluded, warming, ventilatory support, and careful fluids.

cards.q: What is the treatment of severe hypoglycaemia in ICU?
cards.a: Dextrose 50% 25–50 mL (or 10% 150–200 mL) IV, glucagon 1 mg IM if no access, and continuous infusion if recurrent. Target glucose 140–180 mg/dL (7.8–10 mmol/L).

cards.q: What is the glycaemic target for critically ill adults?
cards.a: Start insulin at glucose ≥180 mg/dL (10 mmol/L) and keep 140–180 mg/dL; avoid tight control (NICE-SUGAR).

cards.q: How does euglycaemic DKA present?
cards.a: DKA with glucose <14 mmol/L (250 mg/dL), commonly with SGLT2 inhibitors. Treat with insulin plus dextrose-containing fluids.

cards.q: What is a pheochromocytoma crisis and how is it managed?
cards.a: Paroxysmal hypertension, headache, sweating, arrhythmia. Give alpha blockade first (phentolamine, phenoxybenzamine) then beta blockade; avoid beta-blockers alone.

cards.q: What are the endocrine causes of persistent hypotension in ICU?
cards.a: Adrenal insufficiency (including relative or critical illness-related), hypothyroidism, and rarely pheochromocytoma or hypopituitarism.

cards.q: How is hypercalcaemic crisis diagnosed?
cards.a: Corrected calcium >3.5 mmol/L (14 mg/dL) or symptomatic >3.0 with PTH-related or PTH-independent causes; treat with saline, calcitonin, zoledronic acid, and treat the cause.

cards.q: A patient in DKA has pH 7.1, glucose 520 mg/dL and K⁺ 2.9 mmol/L. What is the next step?
o: Give IV potassium and fluids; hold insulin until K⁺ is above 3.5 mmol/L
cards.e: Insulin drives potassium into cells and can provoke fatal arrhythmias when K⁺ is low. The 2024 consensus delays insulin until K⁺ >3.5 mmol/L and replaces potassium first.

cards.q: A patient on long-term prednisolone presents with vomiting, BP 70/40, Na⁺ 126, K⁺ 5.8. What is the immediate treatment?
o: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV and 0.9% saline resuscitation
Wait for a short synacthen test
cards.e: Suspected adrenal crisis is a life-threatening emergency: treat immediately without waiting for test results.

cards.q: How is DKA severity categorised in the 2024 consensus?
cards.a: Mild: BHB ≤6 mmol/L, pH >7.25, bicarbonate ≥15, alert. Moderate: BHB ≤6, pH 7.0–7.25, bicarbonate 10 to <15, alert or drowsy. Severe: BHB >6, pH <7.0, bicarbonate <10, stupor or coma, managed in ICU. HHS or concurrent critical illness also warrants ICU care.
